title: Teacher MOCKED My Grandson's Taped Shoes. Then I Saw Her Face

scenes.text: Sweetheart, in the fall of two thousand nineteen, my grandson Ben came home from school, went straight to his room, and wouldn't come out for supper. He was ten. And when I finally got him to open the door, he was holding his sneakers, wrapped in silver duct tape. His teacher had held one up in front of the whole class. The next morning, I put on my church coat and went to see her.
scenes.query: boy holding duct taped sneakers sad bedroom
scenes.caption: DUCT TAPE SHOES

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you what that teacher said to me, and what I said back. And what I recognized in her face, sitting across that little desk, that made both of us cry in a fourth-grade classroom. Stay with me, honey, because it goes back to a church basement in nineteen eighty-three.
scenes.query: elementary classroom empty desks morning
scenes.caption: A CHURCH BASEMENT IN 1983

scenes.text: That was a hard year for my son Mark, sweetheart. The factory where he'd worked for eighteen years closed in the spring, and by summer the savings were gone. So Mark and his wife and their two boys moved in with me on Maple Drive, while he looked for work. Six of us in that little house again. I didn't mind one bit. But Mark minded. He was ashamed.
scenes.query: family moving boxes into small house
scenes.caption: SIX OF US AGAIN

scenes.text: And Ben, the younger boy, had grown two sizes since spring. His sneakers had split along the side, and the sole was flapping. He didn't tell anybody, honey, because he knew money was tight, and he didn't want his daddy to feel worse. So he found Harold's old roll of duct tape in the garage and wrapped them up himself. He was so proud of that. He said, look, Grandma, good as new.
scenes.query: child wrapping sneaker with duct tape garage
scenes.caption: GOOD AS NEW

scenes.text: His teacher was a woman named Mrs. Pruitt. Strict, they said, but a good teacher. And that Tuesday, when the class was lining up for recess, she saw Ben's shoes. And she said, Ben, come here. And she made him take one off. And she held it up, in front of twenty-six children, and she said, class, this is what happens when people don't take care of their things.
scenes.query: teacher holding up taped shoe in classroom
scenes.caption: TAKE IT OFF

scenes.text: The children laughed, sweetheart. Of course they did. They were ten. And by lunchtime, they were calling him Duct Tape. A boy kicked his foot under the table to see if the tape would come off. And Ben sat in the bathroom for the whole recess, so nobody could see his feet. He told me all of this in a whisper, sitting on his bed, and he made me promise not to tell his daddy.
scenes.query: boy sitting alone school bathroom
scenes.caption: THEY CALLED HIM DUCT TAPE

scenes.text: If Grandma's story is touching your heart, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. I kept that promise, honey. I didn't tell Mark. But I didn't sleep either. I sat at the kitchen table until two in the morning, with my tea going cold, deciding what I was going to say to that woman. I was seventy-five years old. And I was angrier than I'd been in thirty years.
scenes.query: elderly woman at kitchen table late night tea
scenes.caption: ANGRIER THAN IN 30 YEARS

scenes.text: Around midnight, I went out to the garage and found that roll of duct tape on Harold's workbench, right where Ben had left it. And I stood there holding it, and I thought about Harold, who fixed everything in this house with that tape for forty years. The lawnmower handle, the mailbox, the garden hose. Nobody ever laughed at Harold. They called him handy. I'll tell you why that mattered so much in a minute.
scenes.query: roll of duct tape on old workbench
scenes.caption: THEY CALLED HIM HANDY

scenes.text: I went in the next morning at seven thirty, before the children arrived. I wore my good navy coat and Harold's mother's pearl brooch, because I wanted to look like somebody who should be listened to. The principal was a nice young man, and he looked nervous. He brought me down the hall to Mrs. Pruitt's classroom, and he said, I'll let you two talk. In a minute I'll tell you what I saw on her desk.
scenes.query: elderly woman in navy coat school hallway
scenes.caption: SOMEBODY TO LISTEN TO

scenes.text: Mrs. Pruitt was about forty-five, with her hair pulled back tight and reading glasses on a chain. She stood up and shook my hand like a businessman. And before I could say a word, she said, Mrs. Ruth, I know why you're here. I believe children need to learn responsibility for their belongings. If the shoes were in that condition, someone wasn't taking care of them. That's all I was teaching.
scenes.query: stern teacher with glasses on chain
scenes.caption: RESPONSIBILITY

scenes.text: I sat down in that tiny chair, sweetheart, the kind made for children, with my knees up by my chin. And I said, Mrs. Pruitt, my grandson taped those shoes himself, because his father lost his job, and he didn't want to ask for anything. He wasn't being careless. He was being brave. And you held up his bravery for twenty-six children to laugh at.
scenes.query: elderly woman in small classroom chair
scenes.caption: HE WAS BEING BRAVE

scenes.text: She opened her mouth to argue, honey. And that's when I really looked at her. Something in her face. The shape of her chin, the little gap in her front teeth. And on her desk, in a frame, there was an old photograph of a church I knew. First Lutheran, on Third Street. My church. Harold and I went there for fifty years. I said, did you grow up in Mansfield? She said, yes. Why?
scenes.query: framed photo of small church on teacher's desk
scenes.caption: FIRST LUTHERAN

scenes.text: So far, the duct tape, the classroom, the laughing, and a stern teacher with a photograph of my church on her desk. I said, what was your name before you married? And she said, Kessler. Linda Kessler. And my heart stopped, sweetheart. Because I remembered a Linda Kessler. A skinny little girl with a gap in her teeth, in the basement of First Lutheran, at Christmas, in nineteen eighty-three. Stay with me.
scenes.query: church basement 1980s Christmas tables
scenes.caption: LINDA KESSLER

scenes.text: Every December back then, our church ran a shoe drive. The ladies collected money all year, and we bought new shoes for any child in town who needed them. I was in charge of it for twelve years. We set up in the church basement with a foot measuring stick and boxes stacked to the ceiling, and the children came in with their mothers, one by one. And in nineteen eighty-three, a little girl came in alone.
scenes.query: foot measuring device and shoe boxes
scenes.caption: THE SHOE DRIVE

scenes.text: She was about nine. Her mother hadn't come, she said, because her mother was sick. And when she sat down and I unlaced her shoes, they were wrapped in masking tape, honey. Masking tape, soaked through from the snow. Her socks were wet. Her little toes were red. And she said, very quietly, please don't tell anybody. I don't want them to know.
scenes.query: little girl's shoes wrapped in masking tape
scenes.caption: PLEASE DON'T TELL ANYBODY

scenes.text: I didn't tell anybody. I took her into the back room, away from the other children. I dried her feet with a dish towel and put two pairs of my own wool socks on her. And I gave her the best pair of boots we had, the red ones, with the fur lining, that I'd been saving. And I said, honey, there's no shame in tape. Tape means you're making do. Making do is the bravest thing there is.
scenes.query: red fur lined children's winter boots
scenes.caption: MAKING DO IS BRAVE

scenes.text: I remembered her because she didn't smile once the whole time, sweetheart. Most children were so excited about new shoes that they danced around the basement. Linda just sat very still and looked at the floor. When I laced up the red boots, she touched the fur inside with one finger, like she was afraid it would disappear. And when she left, she walked out the door backwards, so she could keep looking at me. I thought about her for years.
scenes.query: little girl touching fur inside boot
scenes.caption: AFRAID IT WOULD DISAPPEAR

scenes.text: I looked at that teacher across the desk, and I said, Linda, did you have red boots, with fur inside? And her face changed, sweetheart. All that hardness just fell away. She took off her glasses. She said, how do you know about the red boots? And I said, because I put them on your feet. In the back room of First Lutheran. You had masking tape on your shoes.
scenes.query: teacher removing glasses shocked expression
scenes.caption: THE RED BOOTS

scenes.text: She put both hands over her face, honey. And she cried like that nine-year-old girl. She said, I wore those boots for three winters. Until my toes curled. I never told anybody about the tape. Not my husband. Not anybody. I promised myself nobody would ever look at me and see a poor girl again. And then she said, oh, God. I did that to your grandson. I did the exact thing I was afraid of.
scenes.query: woman crying at desk hands over face
scenes.caption: I DID THAT TO HIM

scenes.text: I'll tell you something I've learned in eighty years, sweetheart. People who were ashamed as children are sometimes the hardest on the children who remind them of it. It isn't cruelty, usually. It's fear. When Linda saw that tape on Ben's shoes, she wasn't seeing Ben. She was seeing herself. And she wanted it gone. I took her hand across that little desk, and we both just sat there and cried.
scenes.query: two women holding hands across school desk
scenes.caption: IT WAS FEAR

scenes.text: That afternoon, honey, Mrs. Pruitt did something I'll never forget. She asked Ben to stay in at recess. And she told him she was sorry. And then, the next morning, in front of the whole class, she told them a story about a little girl with masking tape on her shoes, and a lady in a church basement with red boots. And at the end, she said, that little girl was me.
scenes.query: teacher talking to class at front of room
scenes.caption: THAT LITTLE GIRL WAS ME

scenes.text: She said, Ben is the bravest boy in this room. He fixed something himself instead of complaining. And anybody who calls him Duct Tape again will be talking to me. Ben told me the room was so quiet you could hear the clock. And at lunch, the boy who'd kicked his foot sat down next to him and asked him how he wrapped them so tight. They're still friends today.
scenes.query: boys eating lunch together school cafeteria
scenes.caption: THE BRAVEST BOY

scenes.text: And that Christmas, sweetheart, Linda Pruitt opened a shoe closet at that school. A little room by the nurse's office, full of new sneakers and boots in every size, where any child can go, quietly, with no questions and no list of names. She asked if she could name it after me. I said, honey, name it after your mother. She said, no. I want the children to know a stranger did this.
scenes.query: small closet full of new children's shoes
scenes.caption: THE SHOE CLOSET

scenes.text: It's called Ruth's Closet, and it's still there. Mark found work that winter, at a warehouse, and the family moved out in the spring. Ben's sixteen now, and taller than his father. And every December, he and Mrs. Pruitt go to the store together and fill that closet up again. He uses his own money from his summer job. He told me, Grandma, I want somebody to get the red boots.
scenes.query: teenage boy carrying shoe boxes into school
scenes.caption: SOMEBODY GETS THE RED BOOTS

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, honey. Before you laugh at somebody's shoes, think about who taped them, and why. Making do is the bravest thing there is. Tell me in the comments, sweetheart, did you ever have to make do with something as a child? There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: pair of red children's boots by Christmas tree
scenes.caption: MAKING DO IS BRAVE
